title: JavaScript Performance Patterns
summary: The main thread is single and uninterruptible, so every long task is a frozen UI. Debounce, throttle, workers, and yielding are four different answers to the same constraint.

slides.markdown:
One thread runs your JavaScript, your event handlers, style, layout, and paint. It cannot be interrupted. Everything in this topic follows from that single fact.

While a function runs, nothing else happens: no clicks handled, no frames rendered, no scrolling. A 400ms function is a 400ms frozen page — and if the user taps during it, their tap waits the full 400ms before your handler even starts.

The four families of answer:

- **Do the work less often** — debounce and throttle.
- **Do it somewhere else** — Web Workers.
- **Do it in pieces** — yielding, `scheduler.yield()`, `requestIdleCallback`.
- **Do less of it** — memoisation, virtualisation, better algorithms.

The measuring stick throughout is the **50ms long-task threshold** and the **16.7ms frame budget**. Those two numbers decide whether a technique is worth applying.

slides.subTitle: Why 50ms is the line
slides.markdown:
A **long task** is any main-thread task exceeding **50ms**. The number comes from responsiveness research, not from frame rate.

The reasoning chain: the **RAIL** model says a response to user input should land within about **100ms** to feel immediate. Input arriving at the worst possible moment — right as a task starts — waits the whole task. So keeping tasks under 50ms leaves headroom to handle the input and render a response inside 100ms.

What this looks like concretely, for a 300ms task:

- Any tap during it queues for up to 300ms of **input delay** before your handler runs.
- **Roughly 18 frames** are missed, so animations and scrolling freeze.
- The task contributes **250ms of Total Blocking Time** (TBT counts only the excess over 50ms).

And the counter-intuitive fix falls straight out of that formula: **splitting a 300ms task into six 50ms tasks removes all 250ms of TBT while doing exactly the same work.** Total CPU time is identical; what changes is that five yield points now exist where a queued input can be serviced.

That's the core insight of this whole topic — for responsiveness, **task granularity matters more than total work**.

slides.subTitle: Two different questions
slides.markdown:
Both reduce how often a function runs on a rapid event stream, but they answer different questions.

| | Debounce | Throttle |
|---|---|---|
| Rule | run once, `delay` after the events **stop** | run at most once per `interval` **while** events continue |
| Calls during a 3s burst at 100/s | **1** | ~6 at 500ms interval |
| Guarantees a run during the burst | no | yes |
| Latency to the final value | delay after last event | up to one interval |
| Right for | search-as-you-type, autosave, resize-complete | scroll position, mousemove tracking, progress updates |
| Wrong for | anything needing feedback *during* the stream | anything where only the final value matters |

The question that picks between them: **do I need updates while it's happening, or only after it stops?**

- A search box firing a network request: only the final value matters, and firing on every keystroke wastes requests. **Debounce**, ~300ms.
- A scroll-driven progress bar: it must move *during* the scroll, or it's broken. **Throttle**, ~100ms or per animation frame.
- A window-resize handler that re-layouts an expensive chart: **debounce** it, because intermediate sizes are throwaway.
- A drag handler updating an element's position: **throttle** with `requestAnimationFrame`, so it runs exactly once per frame — no more, no less.

slides.subTitle: Seeing the difference
slides.markdown:
Picture a horizontal timeline of scroll events firing roughly every 15ms across a three-second scroll — a dense row of tick marks, then a pause, then more ticks.

On a **debounced** row (300ms), nothing fires during the whole first burst. Only 300ms after the ticks stop does a single execution mark appear. If the user scrolls continuously for ten seconds, the handler runs **zero times** until they stop. For a search request that's ideal; for a progress bar it means the bar never moves.

On a **throttled** row (200ms), an execution mark appears at the very first event, then again every 200ms for as long as ticks keep arriving — evenly spaced, roughly 15 executions across the three seconds, plus usually a trailing one after the last tick.

And an **unthrottled** row is nearly solid: ~200 executions, one per event, which is what makes a heavy scroll handler freeze the page.

The shape to remember: debounce collapses a burst to **one call at the end**; throttle thins it to a **steady rate throughout**.

slides.subTitle: The version interviewers ask you to write
The right throttle for visual work
A genuinely separate thread
slides.markdown:
A **Web Worker** runs JavaScript on a real OS thread, parallel to the main thread. It's the only way to do heavy computation without blocking the UI at all.

What a worker can and can't do:

- **Can**: run any computation, `fetch`, use IndexedDB, use `WebAssembly`, use `OffscreenCanvas` to render.
- **Can't**: touch the DOM, read `window` or `document`, or access most layout APIs. It has its own global scope.

Communication is by **message passing**, and the cost model here is what decides whether a worker is worth it:

- Messages are **structured-cloned** by default — the data is deep-copied. Sending a 50MB object costs a real serialise/deserialise on both ends, and that copy happens *on the main thread*, which is exactly what you were trying to avoid.
- **Transferables** avoid the copy: `postMessage(buf, [buf])` hands an `ArrayBuffer` over in O(1), leaving it unusable on the sender. This is how you move large binary data cheaply.
- **`SharedArrayBuffer`** gives genuinely shared memory, but requires cross-origin isolation headers (COOP/COEP), which is a real deployment constraint.

Good fits: parsing a large CSV or JSON payload, image processing, cryptography, search indexing, diffing large datasets, syntax highlighting.

Bad fits: anything small. Spawning a worker costs a few milliseconds and a few megabytes, and the round trip adds latency. Below roughly **50ms of computation**, the overhead usually exceeds the benefit.

slides.subTitle: Heavy work, responsive UI
Breaking one long task into many short ones
Four techniques, four situations
slides.markdown:
| Situation | Technique | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Event fires 100x/s, only the final value matters | **debounce** | collapses the burst to one call |
| Event fires 100x/s, UI must update during it | **throttle** or rAF-throttle | steady rate, aligned to frames |
| One expensive computation, no DOM needed | **Web Worker** | true parallelism, main thread untouched |
| One expensive computation that touches the DOM | **yield in chunks** | can't leave the main thread, so shorten the tasks |
| Optional background work | **`requestIdleCallback`** | runs only when nothing else needs the thread |
| Recomputing the same result repeatedly | **memoise** | eliminate the work rather than reschedule it |
| Rendering 10,000 rows | **virtualise** | fewer nodes beats faster code |

The hierarchy worth stating explicitly: **eliminate > move > split > reduce frequency.**

Deleting the work (memoisation, virtualisation, a better algorithm) beats everything else. Moving it to a worker is next. Splitting it into chunks keeps the UI alive but doesn't reduce total cost. Debounce and throttle are the weakest tool — they only change how often you pay.

The mistake this ordering prevents is reaching for `debounce` first out of habit. If a filter function takes 400ms on 50,000 rows, debouncing it means the user still waits 400ms with a frozen page — just less often. Making the function fast, or moving it to a worker, is the actual fix.

slides.subTitle: And the other classic mistakes
slides.markdown:
The wrong choice between the two produces bugs that read as "the feature is broken" rather than "the page is slow":

- **Debouncing a scroll-position indicator.** During a continuous 10-second scroll the events never stop, so the handler runs **zero times**. The progress bar sits frozen and only jumps to the right place when the user stops. Needed throttle.
- **Throttling a search request.** With a 300ms throttle, typing "performance" fires four or five requests instead of one — wasted bandwidth, wasted server load, and results that arrive out of order. Needed debounce.
- **Debouncing with too long a delay.** 1000ms on a search box feels broken; the user has finished typing and is staring at nothing. 200-400ms is the usual sweet spot for search, and shorter for validation feedback.
- **Recreating the debounced function on every render.** In React, `debounce(fn, 300)` called inline in the component body produces a fresh timer each render, so nothing is ever actually debounced. It must be wrapped in `useMemo`/`useRef` with a stable identity.
- **Not cancelling on unmount.** A pending debounced callback fires after the component is gone, setting state on a dead component or writing to a stale ref.
- **Debouncing input display.** Debounce the *network request*, never the controlled input's own value — debounced typing feels laggy and broken.

The check that catches all of these: **write down what should happen during a continuous 10-second stream of events.** If the answer is "nothing until it stops," debounce. If it's "keep updating," throttle.

slides.subTitle: The tier above scheduling
slides.markdown:
Scheduling techniques manage cost. These remove it.

- **Memoisation.** Cache by input. A filter recomputed on every render over an unchanged 50,000-row array is pure waste — `useMemo` or a small LRU eliminates it entirely. Watch the cache key: memoising on an object recreated each render caches nothing.
- **Virtualisation.** Render only the visible rows. A 10,000-row table becomes ~30 DOM nodes, which cuts layout, paint, memory, and event handler count all at once. Almost always the right answer above a few hundred rows.
- **Indexing instead of scanning.** A `Map` lookup replaces a repeated `Array.find()`. Building the map once turns an O(n) operation per interaction into O(1) — this is where actual algorithmic knowledge pays off in frontend code.
- **Batching state updates.** Ten `setState` calls that each trigger a render is ten renders; React 18 auto-batches within event handlers, but not always across `await` boundaries.
- **Doing it on the server.** Sorting, filtering, and aggregating a large dataset is often better done where the data lives, sending 50 rows instead of 50,000.
- **Structural sharing.** Cloning a large object on every update (`{...state}` deep) can dominate a handler; immutable libraries share unchanged subtrees.

The interview-relevant framing: when someone asks how to fix a slow handler, **the strongest answer starts by questioning whether the work needs to happen**, and only then discusses scheduling. Candidates who jump straight to `debounce` have skipped the tier that usually contains the real win.

slides.subTitle: Concurrent rendering and where it fits
slides.markdown:
Modern frameworks build task-splitting into rendering itself, which changes what you have to hand-roll.

**React's concurrent features** are the ones most likely to come up:

- **`useTransition`** marks a state update as non-urgent. React renders the urgent part first — the input's own value updating as you type — paints it, then renders the expensive list. That directly targets INP's processing and presentation phases, and on a search-as-you-type field it's often a **300ms → 80ms** change.
- **`useDeferredValue`** is the same idea expressed as a value: the expensive component reads a lagging copy while the input stays instant.
- **Time slicing** lets React interrupt a long render to handle input, then resume — the framework doing what manual yielding does, but with knowledge of what's urgent.

The important nuance: **this is not the same as debouncing.** A transition renders with the *latest* value and abandons obsolete renders; a debounce delays starting. The user sees the input respond instantly either way, but a transition keeps the expensive view as fresh as the CPU allows rather than waiting a fixed 300ms.

Where hand-rolled tools still win: a genuinely CPU-bound computation. Concurrent rendering slices *React's own rendering work* — it does nothing for a 400ms synchronous function you call inside a handler. That still needs a worker, or chunked yielding, or to be made faster.

Knowing that boundary is the difference between using the framework and trusting it to solve problems it can't see.
